title: Chapter 47: Oren's Barrier, Again, Part 3 of 5: The Biggest Thing
html:
The last time, he had not chosen.
At the mouth of the arch, in the autumn, with the log coming at him on its handcart and the men behind it, he had shut his eyes and reached, and taken the first thing that came. Something small. Something from that morning. A word. It had come away in his hand like a loose tooth, and he had burned it, and the wall had come up clear and shining with gold round its edges, and held. And when it was over he had found that he could not say spoon.
That had been a small wall. The mouth of one arch. Two men and a log.
This was a window the width of a shop. Seven men and an iron bar. And a woman with gray gloves who could put her hand on clear light and turn it to frost.
A word would not hold that. He knew it the way you know, when you lift a sack, whether you can carry it to the end of the street. A word would hold for the first blow. Perhaps the second. And then the frost would go into it, and it would go white, and brittle, and crack, the way the glass was cracking now, and the bar would come through, and the men would come through after it. Into the shop. Into the back room. Up the stair.
He needed something big.
He stood in the middle of the cold shop with his eyes shut and his sword across his body in its scabbard, and he went looking through himself for it. Quickly. The way you go through a house that is on fire, looking for the one thing you will carry out.
It was a strange thing, to look at yourself like that. To stand in the middle of your own life and turn round slowly and see what was in it. He had never done it before. He had not known there was so much.
There was his mother. A small fierce woman in a black shawl, throwing two spoons out of a kitchen window into the snow. He could see her face. He could hear her voice. No more of that noise in my house. No more war in my kitchen. He did not reach for her.
There was his brother. A boy of ten with a ramrod back sitting at the end of the kitchen table, silent for weeks, after the march from the north. And then one winter night, picking up the spoons, and showing him. Four. Two. Nine. Three. Over and over, till the candle went out. And then a man on a gray horse on the Lantern Bridge, with silver on his shoulders and a scar in his eyebrow, pinning his hand to the parapet in the snow. Never do that in this city. He did not reach for his brother.
There was Crown Walk. Twenty-two years of it. Every door, every stair, every window, every lock and bolt and bell. The smell of the hall in the mornings, beeswax and coal smoke. The weight of the captain's coat on his shoulders the first day, when he was twenty-four and so proud he could hardly breathe. The Lady Isolde coming down the stairs in gray silk. A small girl of nine, holding his hand at the edge of the park pond and asking why ducks did not get cold feet. A small boy on a gray pony, going round the park on his own for the first time, shouting you let go.
He did not reach for any of it.
He was a guard. A guard keeps the house. He does not burn it to keep the door.
He went on looking.
And behind the house, behind the people, behind the faces and the voices and the rooms, there were other things. Things that were not people. Things he could do. The way his hands knew how to hold a sword and saddle a horse and load a pistol in the dark. The way his feet knew how to march. The way his eyes knew how to count men in a street. He could not burn those. Those were what he used to keep the house.
And among them, small and plain and gray, like a tool that hangs on the wall of a shed and that you take down once a day and put back without thinking about it, there was this.
The letters.
He looked at it.
It was not small. That was the first thing he saw, standing there in the middle of himself with his eyes shut. He had always thought of it as small. A thing he did not much like and was not much good at. But it was not small at all. It was enormous. It went everywhere. It went into every corner of him, like the roots of a tree going down under a house. Every sign he had read today in the snow. CHANDLER. BOOTS MENDED WHILE YOU WAIT. Every order he had ever been given on a piece of paper. Every list. Every name on every door. The cards on Madame Hesper's drawers. BUTTONS, JET. The gold letters on her window. The notice on the corner of Chandler Row. WANTED. And the paper in his pocket. The cream-colored one, folded small, in its square of oilcloth, inside Terrence's coat, against his chest. I, Aurelian Thorne, being of sound mind.
All of it was the letters. All of it was this one plain gray thing that an old woman with a stick had put into him at six years old in a dame school in the north, rapping his knuckles every time he got a shape wrong.
He had not known it was so big.
It was big enough.
He knew that at once, the way you know a sack is light enough to carry. It was big enough to make a wall the width of a window. Big enough to hold against seven men and a bar. Big enough, perhaps, to hold for a while against a woman in gray gloves.
And it was not a person. It was not his mother, or his brother, or the Lady Isolde on the stair, or the girl at the pond. It was not the house. It was only a tool. A thing he could do, that he did not much like doing.
He would never read again.
He thought that, very clearly, standing in the shop with his eyes shut and the frost crackling on the glass in front of him. He would never read again. Not a sign. Not a list. Not a name on a door. Not the paper in his pocket. He would walk through the city and the marks on the boards would be marks, and the notices would be marks, and the cards on the drawers would be marks. Pretty, some of them. Shapes. Like the patterns on the inside of a shell. And nothing in his head when he looked at them. No boots. No buttons. No WANTED. Nothing.
He would be a man who had to be read to.
The iron bar hit the window.
He heard it. A crash, enormous, glass going, a whole pane, two, the old lead bending, and cold air rushing in at him across the shop like water through a broken dam, and snow with it. And the voices of the men, outside, close now. Shouting to each other. Again. Again.
And behind him, at the far end of the house, from the dark passage, the third blow on the green door. And under it, very faint, a woman's voice. Not shouting. Saying something, round a mouthful of pins, in a tone he knew. The tone she had used to him on the step, an hour ago. Is there something wrong with it?
Oren Vance took hold of the letters.
All of them. All at once. The whole plain gray enormous root of it, going down through every corner of him. He took hold of it with both hands, the way you take hold of a rope.
And pulled.
Letters
It did not come away like a tooth.
The word, in the autumn, had come away like a tooth. One quick pull, a small sharp pain, and then a gap. This was not like that. This was like pulling a root out of the ground. A long root, with a great many smaller roots going off it, and smaller roots going off those, down and down through every corner of him. He pulled, and it came, slowly, tearing. And as it came he felt every small root give way, one after another, all through him, in places he had not known it went.
And it burned.
Not in his hands. In his chest. A great bright heat going up, the way a dry hayrick goes up when the lightning hits it. All at once. A roar of it.
He opened his eyes.
The wall was there.
It was standing across the shop, between him and the broken window, from the floor to the ceiling and from wall to wall. Clear as water. So clear that if it had not been for the way the snow stopped against it, the snow blowing in through the broken panes and stopping in the air, a hand's width from the clear wall, and sliding down it, he would not have known it was there. And all round its edges, where it met the floor and the walls and the ceiling, a line of light.
Gold.
The color of honey with the sun in it. The color of a candle flame seen through a closed eyelid. It ran round the whole edge of the clear wall like the gilt edge round a page in a book. Bright and steady and warm. Brighter than it had been in the arch, in the autumn. Much brighter. It filled the cold shop with a soft gold light, so that the bolts of cloth on their shelves glowed, and the gloves in their glass case glowed, and the jet buttons on the floor round his boots glowed like a scattering of black stars.
The iron bar hit it.
Boom.
He felt it in his chest. In his knees. In the back of his skull. The wall went white, all over, for a moment, white as the snow, and bowed inward toward him. And then went clear again. And the bar bounced back off it, and one of the men holding it fell down in the snow on the pavement outside, and the other one swore.
The wall held.
Oren stood behind it with his sword across his body and his feet apart on the buttons, and breathed.
And as he breathed, he looked round the shop. He did not know why. Because his eyes wanted to. Because some part of him that he had just burned was still there, a little, at the edges, like the gold round the wall, and wanted to look while it could.
He looked at the drawers behind the counter.
The little white cards in their little brass frames. Dozens of them. In rows.
BUTTONS, JET.
He could read that one. He read it. Then he read the next one. BUTTONS, PEARL. And the next.
HOOKS &
The next word was not there.
There was something on the card after HOOKS &. Marks. Black. A row of them, the same size as the others, close together. He looked at them. He knew they were letters. He knew they said something. He looked at them very hard, the way you look at a face across a crowded room that you are sure you know. And nothing came. No word. No thing in his head. Just the marks. A round one. A straight one with a cross. A round one again.
HOOKS & and then marks.
He looked at the card above it.
TAPE.
And then marks.
He looked at the card below it.
Marks.
It was going fast now. He could feel it. Like water going out of a basin when somebody has pulled the plug. Faster and faster, round and round. He looked along the row of drawers and the cards went to marks as he looked at them, one after another, from left to right, as if somebody were walking along the row ahead of his eyes and wiping each card clean. BUTTONS, J—marks. Marks. Marks.
The bar hit the wall again. Boom. White. Clear.
He looked at the cloth on the shelves. There were labels pinned to the ends of the bolts. Little paper tags, with writing on them in a small sharp hand. Madame Hesper's hand. He had seen it on the card on the box yesterday. He looked at the tags. Marks. All marks. Pretty ones. Thin and black and slanting, like the tracks of a bird in the snow.
The frost had started on the wall.
He saw it. The tall pale woman had stepped up to the broken window, through the broken glass, and stood with the snow blowing round her, and laid her gray-gloved hand flat on the clear wall. On the inside of the window frame, where the wall met the wood and the gold ran along the edge. And from under her hand the white was spreading. Feathery. Fine. Branching, like the veins of a leaf, like frost on a window on the coldest night of the year. Crackling.
Where it touched the gold, the gold went dim.
And the cold came into him.
He had felt it before. In the arch. He had not forgotten it. But knowing a thing and feeling it again are not the same. It came into his chest through the wall, through the gold, through the place where the letters had been torn out of him and burned, and the place was raw, and open, and the cold went into it like a knife into a wound. He made a sound. He did not mean to. His knees bent. His hands on the sword went white.
The wall held.
He did not know how. He held it. He stood there with the cold in his chest and the frost spreading white across the clear wall in front of him and the men outside lifting the bar again, and he held it, because the letters were burning and the letters were big. So big. Bigger than he had ever known. There was still more of them. There was still a great deal more, going up, roaring, somewhere behind his ribs.
He looked at the window.
At the frame of it, the black wood. At the broken panes, and the ones that were not broken yet, covered in frost. And through the frost, through the clear wall, through the snow, at the gold letters painted on the old glass.
They were still there. On the panes that were not broken. Backward. Curving across the top of the window in an arch.
ELBMIHT DNA ELDEEN EHT.
He could not read them.
He looked at them, and they were marks. Gold marks, curved, beautiful, catching the light of the gas lamp outside and the gold light of his own wall. Pretty. Like the patterns on the inside of a shell. Nothing in his head.
And below them, smaller, on the pane in the middle, the one with the frost spreading across it from the corner where the woman's hand was. The pane with the gold letter H on it that she had touched first.
REPSEH .EMM
He looked at it.
And it was a word.
It was the only one. In the whole of the shop, in the whole of the street, in the whole of the white falling world. He looked along it, from the right, backward, the way he had done it an hour ago standing by his chair. Slowly. Letter by letter. And they were letters. They stayed letters. He did not know why. Perhaps because he had read it twice on the green door in the mews, and liked the shape of the H. Perhaps because she had said Is there something wrong with it? Perhaps because it was the last thing in him that the fire had not reached yet.
H.
Like a little gate.
E. S. P. E. R.
HESPER.
He read it.
And as he read it, in the frost, in the gold light, through the clear wall, he heard, from the far end of the house, through the shop and the back room and the dark passage, a sound.
Not a blow. Not the dull thud of a shoulder on oak.
The crack of wood giving way.
And a woman's voice, round a mouthful of pins. Very clear. Very calm. The voice of somebody who has been dressing the Hill for forty-one years and does not intend to be hurried now.
Not in my shop.
The gold letters on the window went to marks.
He looked at them, and they were marks. The H was a gate no longer. It was two lines with a line across. It was nothing. It was gold paint on old glass.
There was nothing left in him to read with.
And the wall, which had been burning on the last of it, went up one last time, bright, roaring, gold from edge to edge, so bright that the men outside put their arms over their faces and the pale woman with her hand flat on it stepped back. Once.
Only once.
The Wall
After that, it was only holding.
There was nothing new to burn. The letters were gone. All of them. He could feel the place where they had been, a great raw hollow going down through every corner of him like the hole a tree leaves when it is pulled out of the ground. And the fire was still going in it. Still roaring. But it was the roar of a fire that has been fed all it will ever be fed, and is burning down. He knew that. A soldier knows the sound of a fire that is burning down.
He held.
The frost came across the wall in front of him from the corner where the pale woman's hand lay. Slowly now. It had slowed when the gold flared. But it was coming. White, feathery, crackling, branching across the clear surface in long fine lines like the veins on the back of an old hand. Where it went, the wall went stiff. He could feel it go stiff. Like a muscle cramping. Where it touched the gold at the edges, the gold went dim, and the dimness crept along the line of light toward the ceiling and toward the floor, a finger's width at a time.
And every finger's width of it went into his chest, cold.
The bar came again. Boom. The wall went white. Bowed. His knees bent. He straightened them.
Outside, the men had changed what they were doing. They had stopped running at the window with the bar. Two of them had gone to the street door, and he heard them at it, beside him, a few feet away, through the oak. A blade going into the crack between the door and the frame, at the bolt. A grunt. A blade going in at the other bolt. They had not seen that the wall ran across the whole shop, door and window and all, from the street wall to the street wall. They would find out when they got the door open.
The one with the hooked pole was trying the edge of the wall. Where it met the wall of the shop, at the far end of the window. Hooking at it. Trying to get the iron hook round behind the gold line, to pull it away from the stone, the way you pull a sheet off a bed. The hook touched the gold, and the man yelled and dropped the pole and stood shaking his hand in the snow, and the young one with the thin mustache laughed at him, high and frightened.
The pale woman did not laugh. She did not do anything but stand at the broken window in the snow with her hand flat on the clear wall, and look past him, into the back of the shop, at the door to the back room. Her face had nothing in it. Not even waiting.
Oren held.
He did not think about the girl on the stair. He did not think about the ladder behind the trunk, and the skylight, and the heavy glass, and the leads, and the gutter, and the yard with the barrels. He did not let himself. He thought about the wall. About nothing but the wall. The way you think about nothing but the next step, on a long march in the rain, so that you do not think about how many more there are.
But he heard her.
He could not help it. A guard listens. He heard her bare feet on the stair, going up. Round the second turn. The third. Fast. Very fast. And then, very faint, very far above him, through four floors of old house, a scrape. Wood on wood. A trunk being dragged across bare boards.
And then nothing. For a long time. Too long.
It's heavy, Madame Hesper had said. Push hard.
The bar hit the wall. Boom.
And then, from far above, through the roof, through the ceiling, faint and high and sharp, a sound like a pane of glass cracking in the cold. And a scrape. And another. And then the slates.
He heard them. Over his head. Four floors up. The slates of Madame Hesper's roof, shifting under somebody's weight, the way slates do, a dull clinking click, like crockery being stacked. Moving. Away from the skylight. To the left.
Along the leads, to the left, over two roofs.
He breathed out.
And as he breathed out, the frost reached the ceiling.
It went across the top of the wall from one side to the other, along the gold line, all at once, the way frost goes across a pond in the last hour before dawn. The gold at the top went dim. Almost out. A thin brown thread of light, like the last of a lamp wick. And the cold came down through it into Oren's head. Into the back of his skull. Into his eyes. The shop went gray. The gold light round him went gray. The jet buttons round his boots went gray, and the bolts of cloth, and the gloves praying in their glass case.
He went down on one knee.
He did not mean to. His leg went, the way a leg goes when you have been standing too long in the cold. His knee hit the boards among the buttons, hard. The sword in its scabbard, across his body, shook in his hands.
The wall held.
It was white now. Nearly all of it. From the frost at the top to the frost spreading up from the bottom, where the pale woman had knelt down too, without any hurry, and laid her other gloved hand flat on the clear wall at the level of the floor. White, and stiff, and crackling, and he could hardly see through it. He could see the shapes of the men, dark and blurred, like shapes seen through the window of a steamed-up kitchen. He could see the pale shape of the woman, kneeling, with her two hands on the wall, one high, one low, the way you put your hands on a door to push it.
She was going to push.
He knew it, the way you know, in a fight, a half breath before the other man moves, where the blow is going to come from. She was going to push, with both hands, with the cold, and the wall was going to go. Not crack. Go. All at once. Shatter, like the skin of frozen water on a pond when a stone goes through it.
And behind him, at the far end of the house, where the green door had given way, he heard the other sound.
He heard it through the whole of the house, through the dark passage and the back room and the door, through the cold and the roar of the dying fire in his chest. Not loud. A heavy sound. A sound like something heavy falling against a door. And then a sliding sound. And then nothing.
And then footsteps.
Heavy. Slow. Coming along the dark passage from the green door. Into the back room. Big feet, in big boots. He heard the floorboards give under them. He heard the long table in the back room scrape on the floor as something big knocked into it. He heard one of the dummies go over, a hollow wooden crash.
And then the footsteps stopped.
And turned.
Not toward the shop. Not toward him.
Toward the stair.
Oren Vance knelt among the jet buttons with the white wall in front of him and the pale woman's hands on it, and the frost in his skull, and the last brown thread of gold going out along the top of the wall like a wick.
And behind him, the heavy footsteps began to go up the stair.
Up. Toward the attic. Toward the trunk, and the ladder, and the open skylight with the snow coming down through it, and the leads beyond, and the slates.
He had to choose.
He had chosen, once already, today. He had stood in the middle of himself and turned round and chosen what to burn. He had been a long time choosing. Now there was no time at all. There was the wall in front of him, with seven men and a woman behind it. And the stair behind him, with one man on it, going up.
A guard keeps the house.
But he does not keep the house for the house's sake.
Oren let go of the wall.
He did it the way you let go of a rope you have been holding for a long time. All at once. His hands opened. And the fire in his chest, the last of the letters, went out.
The wall did not crack. It did not shatter. It went up. All at once, from edge to edge, into a cloud of gold. Gold dust. Fine as flour. Bright as sparks. It hung in the air of the shop for one breath, glittering, between him and the broken window, so bright and so thick that the men outside cried out and threw their arms over their faces, and the pale woman, kneeling, with her two hands on nothing, fell forward onto them in the snow.
And then it fell. Like snow. Gold snow, falling slowly in the cold shop, onto the counter and the bolts of cloth and the gloves in their case and the scattered jet buttons on the floor.
Oren was already gone. Through the gold. Through the door to the back room. With his sword out of its scabbard now, bare, in his hand. Toward the stair.
